claim: U1 snRNP binds to the 5′ exon-intron junction of pre-mRNA.
source: U1 snRNP binds to the 5′ exon-intron junction of pre-mRNA and thus plays a crucial role at an early stage of pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and references.

claim: U1 snRNP plays a crucial role at an early stage of pre-mRNA splicing.
source: U1 snRNP binds to the 5′ exon-intron junction of pre-mRNA and thus plays a crucial role at an early stage of pre-mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of RNA splicing.

claim: Two crystal structures of engineered U1 sub-structures were determined.
source: We present two crystal structures of engineered U1 sub-structures, which together reveal at atomic resolution an almost complete network of protein–protein and RNA-protein interactions within U1 snRNP
evidence: The manuscript describes the determination of two crystal structures as the primary experimental work.

claim: The two crystal structures reveal at atomic resolution an almost complete network of protein–protein and RNA-protein interactions within U1 snRNP.
source: We present two crystal structures of engineered U1 sub-structures, which together reveal at atomic resolution an almost complete network of protein–protein and RNA-protein interactions within U1 snRNP
evidence: This is based on the structural data obtained from the crystal structures.

claim: The zinc-finger of U1-C interacts with the duplex between pre-mRNA and the 5′-end of U1 snRNA.
source: The zinc-finger of U1-C interacts with the duplex between pre-mRNA and the 5′-end of U1 snRNA.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The binding of the RNA duplex is stabilized by hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions between U1-C and the RNA backbone around the splice junction.
source: The binding of the RNA duplex is stabilized by hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions between U1-C and the RNA backbone around the splice junction but U1-C makes no base-specific contacts with pre-mRNA.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure showing specific interactions.

claim: U1-C makes no base-specific contacts with pre-mRNA.
source: The binding of the RNA duplex is stabilized by hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions between U1-C and the RNA backbone around the splice junction but U1-C makes no base-specific contacts with pre-mRNA.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The selection of 5′-splice site nucleotides by U1 snRNP is achieved predominantly through basepairing with U1 snRNA.
source: The structure, together with RNA binding assays, shows that the selection of 5′-splice site nucleotides by U1 snRNP is achieved predominantly through basepairing with U1 snRNA whilst U1-C fine-tunes relative affinities of mismatched 5′-splice sites.
evidence: This conclusion is based on both structural data and binding assays.

claim: U1-C fine-tunes relative affinities of mismatched 5′-splice sites.
source: The structure, together with RNA binding assays, shows that the selection of 5′-splice site nucleotides by U1 snRNP is achieved predominantly through basepairing with U1 snRNA whilst U1-C fine-tunes relative affinities of mismatched 5′-splice sites.
evidence: This is supported by binding assays comparing U1 snRNP with and without U1-C.

claim: The spliceosome consists of five small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6 snRNPs) and numerous non-snRNP proteins.
source: This process is catalysed by a large and dynamic RNA-protein assembly called the spliceosome, which consists of five small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6 snRNPs) and numerous non-snRNP proteins (Will and Lührmann, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: U1 snRNP recognizes a short sequence at the 5′-splice site of pre-mRNA through basepairing between the 5′-end of U1 snRNA and the 5′SS sequence.
source: U1 snRNP recognizes a short sequence at the 5′-splice site (5′SS) of pre-mRNA through basepairing between the 5′-end of U1 snRNA and the 5′SS sequence (Lerner et al., 1980; Zhuang and Weiner, 1986; Siliciano and Guthrie, 1988; Séraphin et al., 1988)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: U1 snRNP promotes an ordered assembly of the four remaining snRNPs to form the spliceosome.
source: U1 snRNP recognizes a short sequence at the 5′-splice site (5′SS) of pre-mRNA through basepairing between the 5′-end of U1 snRNA and the 5′SS sequence (Lerner et al., 1980; Zhuang and Weiner, 1986; Siliciano and Guthrie, 1988; Séraphin et al., 1988) and promotes an ordered assembly of the four remaining snRNPs to form the spliceosome
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: During spliceosome activation, the interaction between U1 snRNP and the 5′SS is disrupted by RNA helicase Prp28.
source: During activation, the interaction between U1 snRNP and the 5′SS is disrupted by RNA helicase Prp28 (Staley and Guthrie, 1999)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: After U1 snRNP disruption, the 5′SS intron sequence base-pairs with part of the ACAGAGA box in U6 snRNA.
source: During activation, the interaction between U1 snRNP and the 5′SS is disrupted by RNA helicase Prp28 (Staley and Guthrie, 1999) and then the 5′SS intron sequence base-pairs with part of the ACAGAGA box in U6 snRNA (Sawa and Abelson, 1992; Sawa and Shimura, 1992; Wassarman and Steitz, 1992; Kandels-Lewis and Séraphin, 1993; Lesser and Guthrie, 1993; Sontheimer and Steitz, 1993)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The 5′ exon interacts with U5 snRNA loop I for the first trans-esterification reaction.
source: whilst the 5′ exon interacts with U5 snRNA loop I for the first trans-esterification reaction (Newman and Norman, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: U1 snRNP is an important regulator of mRNA 3′ end cleavage and polyadenylation.
source: U1 snRNP is also an important regulator of mRNA 3′ end cleavage and polyadenylation (Almada et al., 2013; reviewed in Spraggon and Cartegni (2013)).
evidence: This is supported by citations to research papers.

claim: Human U1 snRNP comprises U1 snRNA, seven Sm proteins (SmB/SmB′, SmD1, SmD2, SmD3, SmE, SmF and SmG) and three U1-specific proteins (U1-70K, U1-A and U1-C).
source: Human U1 snRNP comprises U1 snRNA, seven Sm proteins (SmB/SmB′, SmD1, SmD2, SmD3, SmE, SmF and SmG) and three U1-specific proteins (U1-70K, U1-A and U1-C) (Hinterberger et al., 1983; Bringmann and Lührmann, 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A previous structure of the functional core of U1 snRNP was reported based on an experimental electron density map at 5.5 Å resolution.
source: We reported the structure of the functional core of U1 snRNP (Pomeranz Krummel et al., 2009) based on an experimental electron density map at 5.5 Å resolution to which we fitted previously-determined structures of protein components (Kambach et al., 1999; Muto et al., 2004; Leung, 2005).
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: The N-terminal region of U1-70k extends from its RRM through a long α-helix and wraps around the Sm protein assembly.
source: The most striking feature of the structure is the N-terminal region of U1-70k, which extends from its RRM through a long α-helix and wraps around the Sm protein assembly so that its N-terminus makes contact with U1-C protein
evidence: This was observed in the previous 5.5 Å structure.

claim: The N-terminus of U1-70k makes contact with U1-C protein.
source: The most striking feature of the structure is the N-terminal region of U1-70k, which extends from its RRM through a long α-helix and wraps around the Sm protein assembly so that its N-terminus makes contact with U1-C protein
evidence: This was observed in the previous 5.5 Å structure.

claim: U1-70k is required for U1-C binding.
source: The most striking feature of the structure is the N-terminal region of U1-70k, which extends from its RRM through a long α-helix and wraps around the Sm protein assembly so that its N-terminus makes contact with U1-C protein, thus accounting for the requirement of U1-70k for U1-C binding (Nelissen et al., 1994; Hilleren et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations and structural observations.

claim: In the previous 5.5 Å crystal, the 5′-end of U1 snRNA pairs with its symmetry-related counterpart, mimicking the binding of the 5′SS of pre-mRNA to U1 snRNP.
source: In this crystal the 5′-end of U1 snRNA pairs with its symmetry-related counterpart, mimicking the binding of the 5′SS of pre-mRNA to U1 snRNP.
evidence: This describes a feature of the previous crystal structure.

claim: The low-resolution map of the previous structure was insufficient for analysis of the RNA-protein contacts in atomic detail.
source: The Zn-finger domain of U1-C is located adjacent to this RNA duplex but the low-resolution map was insufficient for analysis of the RNA-protein contacts in atomic detail and hence it was not clear how U1-C contributes to the recognition of the 5′SS.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors regarding their previous work.

claim: A structure of U1 snRNP from HeLa cells treated with chymotrypsin was subsequently reported.
source: The structure of U1 snRNP from HeLa cells, treated with chymotrypsin, was subsequently reported (Weber et al., 2010).
evidence: This refers to work by other researchers.

claim: In the chymotrypsin-treated U1 snRNP crystal, the N-terminal end of U1-70k together with U1-C protein were lost by protease treatment.
source: Although this crystal had a DNA oligonucleotide with the 5′SS consensus sequence bound to the 5′-end of U1 snRNA, the N-terminal end of U1-70k together with U1-C protein were lost by protease treatment.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the Weber et al. structure.

claim: Neither the 5.5 Å structure nor the chymotrypsin-treated structure revealed molecular details of 5′SS recognition by U1 snRNP.
source: Hence neither of these structures revealed molecular details of 5′SS recognition by U1 snRNP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of both previous structures.

claim: The inherent mobility of long RNA helices arranged as a 4-way junction prevented the formation of well-diffracting crystals.
source: In order to gain crucial insight into the mechanism of 5′SS recognition we continued our attempts to grow crystals of U1 snRNP diffracting to high resolution but this proved unsuccessful because the inherent mobility of long RNA helices arranged as a 4-way junction prevented the formation of well-diffracting crystals (Oubridge et al., 2009; Weber et al., 2010).
evidence: This explains why the authors designed sub-structures instead of crystallizing the full complex.

claim: Two sub-structures of U1 snRNP with exclusively human sequences were designed based on the 5.5 Å resolution structure.
source: Hence we designed two sub-structures of U1 snRNP, with exclusively human sequences, based on our 5.5 Å resolution structure and determined their crystal structures at high resolution.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in this study.

claim: The sequence of the 5′-single stranded region of U1 snRNA (nts 1–10) is invariant from yeast to human.
source: However, despite these differences, the sequence of the 5′-single stranded region of U1 snRNA (nts 1–10) is invariant from yeast to human (http://rfam.sanger.ac.uk/)
evidence: This is based on sequence database information.

claim: The amino acid sequence of the Zn-finger of U1-C (yeast Yhc1) is highly conserved.
source: and the amino acid sequence of the Zn-finger of U1-C (yeast Yhc1) is also highly conserved (Muto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The 5′SS of pre-mRNA is expected to make exactly the same contacts with the 5′ end of U1 snRNA and U1-C in human and yeast U1 snRNPs.
source: Hence the 5′SS of pre-mRNA is expected to make exactly the same contacts with the 5′ end of U1 snRNA and U1-C in human and yeast U1 snRNPs.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation.

claim: Some positions of the 5′SS have quite different nucleotide bias in yeast and human genes.
source: However, some positions of the 5′SS have quite different nucleotide bias in yeast and human genes (Burge et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: In human, the 5′SS sequences processed by major spliceosomes are degenerate but show significant overall complementarity to the sequence of the 5′ end of U1 snRNA.
source: In human the 5′SS sequences processed by major spliceosomes are degenerate but show significant overall complementarity to the sequence of the 5′ end of U1 snRNA (Lerner et al., 1980).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The 5′SS intron sequence of yeast pre-mRNA is stringently conserved to be GUAUGU.
source: In contrast the 5′SS intron sequence of yeast pre-mRNA is stringently conserved to be GUAUGU (Burge et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Upon activation of the yeast spliceosome, the intron sequence UGU (+4, +5 and +6) pairs with ACA within the ACAGAGA sequence in U6 snRNA.
source: Upon activation of the yeast spliceosome, the intron sequence, UGU (+4, +5 and +6), pairs with ACA within the ACAGAGA sequence in U6 snRNA and hence these nucleotides are selected to be nearly invariant (Sawa and Abelson, 1992; Kandels-Lewis and Séraphin, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The nucleotides at positions +4, +5, and +6 of yeast 5′SS are selected to be nearly invariant because they pair with U6 snRNA.
source: Upon activation of the yeast spliceosome, the intron sequence, UGU (+4, +5 and +6), pairs with ACA within the ACAGAGA sequence in U6 snRNA and hence these nucleotides are selected to be nearly invariant (Sawa and Abelson, 1992; Kandels-Lewis and Séraphin, 1993).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pairing requirement.

claim: Cross-linking studies revealed interaction of the same regions of U6 snRNA and the 5′SS sequence in human.
source: Cross-linking studies revealed interaction of the same regions of U6 snRNA and the 5′SS sequence in human but the sequence requirement is less obvious (Sawa and Shimura, 1992; Wassarman and Steitz, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cross-linking studies.

claim: The two new crystals together reveal the structures of substantial parts of U1 snRNP at high resolution.
source: Our two new crystals together reveal the structures of the substantial parts of U1 snRNP at high resolution and provide crucial insights into the mechanism of pre-mRNA recognition by U1 snRNP.
evidence: This is based on the structural data obtained.

claim: U1-C makes no base-specific contacts with the 5′SS sequence.
source: In particular, we find that U1-C makes no base-specific contacts with the 5′SS sequence.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A minimal U1 snRNP was designed consisting of seven Sm proteins, the N-terminal peptide of U1-70k, U1-C and a truncated U1 snRNA.
source: A minimal U1 snRNP consisting of seven Sm proteins, the N-terminal peptide of U1-70k, U1-C and a truncated U1 snRNA was designed based on the 5.5 Å resolution structure (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2) (Pomeranz Krummel et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental design based on previous structural knowledge.

claim: A large portion of RNA attached to Helix H through the 4-way junction was replaced by a kissing-loop to facilitate crystal contacts.
source: A large portion of RNA attached to Helix H through the 4-way junction was replaced by a kissing-loop (Ennifar et al., 2001) to facilitate crystal contacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a design strategy for crystallization.

claim: The N-terminal 59 residue peptide of U1-70k was fused to SmD1 via a Gly–Ser linker to stabilize its binding.
source: In order to stabilize its binding we fused the N-terminal 59 residue peptide of U1-70k to SmD1 via a Gly–Ser linker (70kSmD1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes an experimental strategy.

claim: The reconstituted minimal U1 snRNP complex was stable and yielded crystals diffracting to 3.3 Å.
source: The reconstituted complex was stable and yielded crystals diffracting to 3.3 Å (Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from crystallization.

claim: The second crystal (U1A70kF-RNA) contains residues 60–216 of U1-70k and the entire U1 snRNA stem-loop I.
source: The second crystal (U1A70kF-RNA) contains residues 60–216 of U1-70k and the entire U1 snRNA stem-loop I.
evidence: This describes the composition of the second crystal.

claim: The U1-70k fragment was fused to the U1-A RRM to promote interaction of the long α-helix with the RNA stem.
source: In order to promote interaction of the long α-helix of U1-70k with the RNA stem we fused it to the U1-A RRM and capped the RNA with the apical loop of stem-loop II such that the α-helix is anchored to the RNA stem (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This describes an experimental design strategy.

claim: The crystal structure of the U1A70kF-RNA complex was determined at 2.5 Å.
source: The crystal structure of this complex was determined at 2.5 Å (Figure 1B; Table 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from crystallography.

claim: Phases for both crystal structures were determined by molecular replacement.
source: Phases for both crystal structures were determined by molecular replacement.
evidence: This describes the crystallographic method used.

claim: The structure of the minimal U1 snRNP fits well into the 5.5 Å electron density except for a slight tilt of the duplex between pre-mRNA and the 5′-end of U1 snRNA.
source: The structure of the minimal U1 snRNP fits well into the 5.5 Å electron density except for a slight tilt of the duplex between pre-mRNA and the 5′-end of U1 snRNA (Figure 1C) (Pomeranz Krummel et al., 2009).
evidence: This compares the new structure with the previous lower-resolution structure.

claim: The fortuitous interaction between the 5′-end of U1 snRNA from two symmetry-related complexes in the previous structure could have distorted the orientation of the RNA duplex.
source: In the previous structure the fortuitous interaction between the 5′-end of U1 snRNA from two symmetry-related complexes could have distorted the orientation of this RNA duplex.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential artifact in the previous structure.

claim: The minimal U1 snRNP with the consensus 5′SS oligonucleotide bound represents the 5′SS-U1 snRNP interaction in the whole U1 snRNP.
source: Hence we believe that the minimal U1 snRNP, with the consensus 5′SS oligonucleotide bound to the 5′-end of U1 snRNA, represents the 5′SS-U1 snRNP interaction in the whole U1 snRNP.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with the previous structure.

claim: The overall structure of the core domain is very similar to that of the U4 snRNP core domain.
source: The overall structure of the core domain is very similar to that of the U4 snRNP core domain, which consists of seven Sm proteins and U4 snRNA (Leung et al., 2011)
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The Sm folds of the seven Sm protein assemblies of U1 and U4 snRNPs superimpose with rmsd of 0.55 Å.
source: and the Sm folds of the seven Sm protein assemblies of the two structures (PDB code: 4PJO and 4WZJ) superimpose with rmsd of 0.55 Å.
evidence: This is quantitative structural comparison data.

claim: In the minimal U1 snRNP, helix H0 of SmD2 points into the minor groove of helix H, buttressing it.
source: In the minimal U1 snRNP, helix H0 of SmD2 points into the minor groove of helix H (Figure 1A), buttressing it, a feature already evident at 5.5 Å (Pomeranz Krummel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The nonamer Sm site sequence has been reported as a minimal RNA oligonucleotide to promote Sm core domain assembly.
source: The nonamer Sm site sequence (AAUUUGUGG in U1 snRNA and AAUUUUUGA in U4 snRNA) has been reported as a minimal RNA oligonucleotide to promote Sm core domain assembly (Raker et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In U1 snRNP, each base of the first seven nucleotides of the nonamer (A125 to U131) interacts one-to-one with SmF-SmE-SmG-SmD3-SmB-SmD1-SmD2 except for the interaction of G130 with SmD1.
source: In U1 snRNP each base of the first seven nucleotides of the nonamer, AAUUUGU (A125 to U131), interacts one-to-one with SmF-SmE-SmG-SmD3-SmB-SmD1-SmD2 in the pockets formed by four key residues at equivalent positions in the L3 and L5 loops of the Sm fold except for the interaction of G130 with SmD1 (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: In the protease-treated U1 snRNP structure, G132 was incorrectly placed in the nucleotide-binding pocket in SmF.
source: In the protease-treated U1 snRNP structure (Weber et al., 2010), G132 was placed in the nucleotide-binding pocket in SmF but our structure unambiguously shows that A125 occupies this pocket.
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous structure showing an error in that structure.

claim: The U4 core snRNP structure has been refined to an Rfree of 22.4%.
source: The U4 core snRNP structure has now been refined to an Rfree of 22.4% (Li, Leung, YK, CO and KN, manuscript in preparation; PDB code: 4WZJ)
evidence: This refers to unpublished work by the authors.

claim: The Sm site nucleotides bind in a similar manner in both minimal U1 and U4 core domain, except for SmD1.
source: and the new model shows that whereas previously the G equivalent to G132 was also incorrectly placed in SmF (Leung et al., 2011) the Sm site nucleotides bind in a similar manner in both minimal U1 and U4 core domain, except for SmD1.
evidence: This is based on comparison of refined structures.

claim: The fourth U of the U4 Sm site sequence is replaced by G in U1 snRNA in the majority of species including humans.
source: The fourth U of the U4 Sm site sequence is replaced by G in U1 snRNA in the majority of species including humans (http://rfam.sanger.ac.uk/) (Burge et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on sequence database information.

claim: A large guanine base cannot be accommodated in SmD1 and hence G130 lies above His37 of SmB outside the central hole.
source: A large guanine base cannot be accommodated in SmD1 and hence it lies above His37 of SmB outside the central hole (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and explained by steric constraints.

claim: The phosphate groups of A126, U130 and U131 come close and are stabilized by a hydrated Mg++ ion.
source: In the Sm site sequence the phosphate groups of A126, U130 and U131 come close and are stabilized by a hydrated Mg++ ion (Figure 2).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The last two nucleotides of the nonamer, G132 and G133, fit into the binding pocket formed by SmD1-SmD2 and SmF-SmE, respectively.
source: The last two nucleotides of the nonamer, G132 and G133, fit into the binding pocket formed by SmD1-SmD2 and SmF-SmE, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Almost the entire length of the U1-70k N-terminal peptide is well ordered in the 3.3 Å structure.
source: In the 3.3 Å structure almost the entire length of the U1-70k N-terminal peptide is well ordered and its interaction with the core domain is revealed in detail (Figure 3).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Residues 49–58 of U1-70k, containing a type II proline helix, interact exclusively with SmD2.
source: Residues 49–58, containing a type II proline helix (Pro55, Pro56 and Pro57), interact exclusively with SmD2 and its binding to SmD2 is stabilized by salt-bridges and hydrogen bonds (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: U1-70k residues 39–49 are wedged in the crevice between SmD2 and SmF.
source: The U1-70k residues 39–49 are wedged in the crevice between SmD2 and SmF (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The U1-70k peptide crosses the central hole where it interacts with the backbone and bases of stem IV (A135 to G138) of U1 snRNA.
source: Then the U1-70k peptide crosses the central hole where it interacts with the backbone and bases of stem IV (A135 to G138) of U1 snRNA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The 3′ stem of U4 snRNA (stem II) blocks the path of the U1-70k peptide in the U4 core domain.
source: The 3′ stem of U4 snRNA (stem II) blocks the path of the U1-70k peptide in the U4 core domain and hence the binding of this peptide is snRNA dependent (Leung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with U4 snRNP.

claim: The binding of the U1-70k peptide is snRNA dependent.
source: The 3′ stem of U4 snRNA (stem II) blocks the path of the U1-70k peptide in the U4 core domain and hence the binding of this peptide is snRNA dependent (Leung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference from structural comparison.

claim: U1-70k residues 10–31 make extensive contacts as an extended peptide with SmD3 and the β4 strand of SmB.
source: The U1-70k residues 10–31 make extensive contacts as an extended peptide with SmD3 and the β4 strand of SmB (Figure 3D; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Residues 6–12 of U1-70k form a 310 helix.
source: The residues 6–12 of U1-70k form a 310 helix and together with its N-terminal region contact the long helix B of U1-C to stabilize U1-C binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The N-terminal region of U1-70k contacts the long helix B of U1-C to stabilize U1-C binding.
source: The residues 6–12 of U1-70k form a 310 helix and together with its N-terminal region contact the long helix B of U1-C to stabilize U1-C binding (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Apart from the interaction with U1-70k, U1-C interacts exclusively with SmD3.
source: Apart from the interaction with U1-70k, U1-C interacts exclusively with SmD3.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Helix A and β1 of the Zn-finger and part of long Helix B of U1-C sit on the concave surface of SmD3.
source: Helix A and β1 of the Zn-finger and part of long Helix B of U1-C sit on the concave surface of SmD3 made by the N-terminal helix 1, β2 strand and loop 2 and a short α-helix made by the C-terminal tail.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The interface between U1-C and SmD3 is not tightly packed and is stabilized by salt-bridges and hydrogen bonds.
source: The interface between U1-C and SmD3 is not tightly packed and is stabilized by salt-bridges and hydrogen bonds (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The R21Q mutation in U1-C weakens its binding to U1 snRNP by about 10-fold.
source: The R21Q mutation in U1-C weakens its binding to U1 snRNP by about 10-fold (Muto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Natural U1 snRNA has a tri-methyl-guanosine cap attached to the 5′-end.
source: Natural U1 snRNA has a tri-methyl-guanosine cap attached to the 5′-end but our U1 snRNA has a 5′-triphosphate resulting from in vitro transcription instead (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about natural U1 snRNA.

claim: The U1 snRNA used in this study has a 5′-triphosphate resulting from in vitro transcription instead of a tri-methyl-guanosine cap.
source: Natural U1 snRNA has a tri-methyl-guanosine cap attached to the 5′-end but our U1 snRNA has a 5′-triphosphate resulting from in vitro transcription instead (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental material used.

claim: Natural U1 snRNA has pseudo-uridines at positions 5 and 6.
source: It also has uridines at positions 5 and 6 instead of the pseudo-uridines found in natural U1 snRNA (Reddy et al., 1981).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The U1 snRNA used in this study has uridines at positions 5 and 6 instead of pseudo-uridines.
source: It also has uridines at positions 5 and 6 instead of the pseudo-uridines found in natural U1 snRNA (Reddy et al., 1981).
evidence: This describes the experimental material used.

claim: Pseudo-uridines at positions 5 and 6 are conserved from yeast to human U1 snRNA.
source: Pseudo-uridines at these positions are conserved from yeast to human U1 snRNA (Massenet et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Only poorly diffracting crystals were obtained with pseudo-uridines at positions 5 and 6.
source: Only poorly diffracting crystals were obtained with pseudo-uridines at these positions.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: In the minimal U1 snRNP crystal, nucleotides 3 to 10 of U1 snRNA form Watson-Crick basepairs with the AG/GUAAGU sequence of the pre-mRNA strand.
source: In the minimal U1 snRNP crystal, nucleotides 3 to 10 of U1 snRNA form Watson-Crick basepairs with the AG/GUAAGU sequence of the pre-mRNA strand (Figure 4B–C) where / marks the splice junction.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The minor groove of the RNA duplex between the 5′SS and the 5′-end of U1 snRNA interacts with U1-C on the surface made by Helix A and the β1 strand.
source: The minor groove of the RNA duplex between the 5′SS and the 5′-end of U1 snRNA interacts with U1-C on the surface made by Helix A and the β1 strand.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Several amino-acid side chains and main chain atoms of U1-C form hydrogen bonds with the 2′OH groups and phosphate oxygen atoms of both strands of RNA near the splice junction.
source: Several amino-acid side chains and main chain atoms of U1-C form hydrogen bonds with the 2′OH groups and phosphate oxygen atoms of both strands of RNA near the splice junction (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A double mutant (R28G, K29S) of U1-C fails to enhance the formation of E complex.
